content: The use of Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is anticipated to rise as women experiencing menopausal symptoms increasingly seek alternative therapies due to concerns about the adverse effects associated with hormone therapy (HT). Scientific evidence is required to assess the effectiveness and safety of CHM in this context. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of CHM for menopausal symptoms, a systematic review was conducted. The search included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, AMED, PsycINFO, and others, covering studies from their inception to March 2015. Additional resources included conference abstracts, reference lists, and direct communication with study authors. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CHM with placebo, HT, pharmaceutical drugs, acupuncture, or other CHM formulations in women aged 18 years or older with menopausal symptoms. A total of 22 RCTs involving 2,902 women were included in the analysis. Most participants were of Chinese origin, though individuals from other ethnic backgrounds were also represented. When CHM was compared to placebo in eight RCTs, there was little to no evidence of a difference between the groups in terms of the number of daily hot flushes (mean difference [MD] 0.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.88 to 0.89; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in hot flushes assessed by an overall hot flush score (MD -0.81 points, 95% CI -2.08 to 0.45; low-quality evidence) or in vasomotor symptoms measured by the Menopause-Specific Quality of Life questionnaire (MD -0.42 points, 95% CI -1.52 to 0.68; low-quality evidence). Individual studies also showed no significant differences between CHM and placebo for daily hot flush severity (MD -0.70 points, 95% CI -1.00 to -0.40; moderate-quality evidence), monthly hot flush scores (MD -2.80 points, 95% CI -8.93 to 3.33; very low-quality evidence), daily night sweats scores (MD 0.07 points, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.33; low-quality evidence), or monthly night sweats scores (MD 1.30 points, 95% CI -1.76 to 4.36; very low-quality evidence). However, one study using the Kupperman Index reported lower monthly vasomotor symptom scores in the CHM group (MD -4.79 points, 95% CI -5.52 to -4.06; low-quality evidence). When CHM was compared to HT in 10 RCTs, only two studies reported monthly vasomotor symptoms using the Menopause-Specific Quality of Life questionnaire. The results were inconclusive regarding whether CHM reduces vasomotor symptoms (MD 0.47 points, 95% CI -0.50 to 1.44; very low-quality evidence). Adverse effects were not consistently reported across the included studies. Among the reported adverse events for CHM were mild diarrhea, breast tenderness, gastric discomfort, and an unpleasant taste. The safety profile of CHM compared to placebo, HT, or specific conventional medications (e.g., fluoxetine, estazolam) was inconclusive due to imprecise effect estimates. For example, the relative risk (RR) of adverse effects for CHM versus placebo was 1.51 (95% CI 0.69 to 3.33; moderate heterogeneity, I² = 40%), for CHM versus HT was 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.39; no heterogeneity, I² = 0%), and for CHM versus specific medications was 0.20 (95% CI 0.03 to 1.17; high heterogeneity, I² = 61%). In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether CHM is more or less effective than placebo or HT for alleviating vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause. The safety profile of CHM remains unclear. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, highlighting the need for well-designed randomized controlled trials to provide more definitive conclusions.
